evidence: Invite students to turn and talk with an elbow partner: 'What is one piece of new information you learned about patterns of the moon?'
rationale: The standard decomposes into four collaborative acts joined by commas (an OR-like list of collaborative purposes). Students work with others to discuss topics through repeated turn-and-talk partner exchanges, e.g., "Invite students to turn and talk with an elbow partner: 'What is one piece of new information you learned about patterns of the moon?'" and "Invite students to turn and talk with an elbow partner: 'What did you notice about the appearance of the moon as it circled around?'" Students also collaboratively investigate the guiding question during the moon-phase simulation where half the class participates while the other half observes, and students "name the phases of the moon as they see the change occur." However, there is no collaborative problem-solving activity, and students do not collaboratively explore or create texts — the Sky Notebook writing is independent, not collaborative. Because the standard lists four collaborative purposes joined by commas and "and," treating them as separable skills requiring all four for full, the lesson meets two but not all → partial.
standard_raw_text: Work with others to discuss topics, investigate questions, solve problems, and explore and create texts. (I/C)

evidence: 'What is one piece of new information you learned about patterns of the moon?' (Responses will vary, but may include: the moon seems to change shape, the moon isn't actually changing.)
rationale: The standard 1.P.EICC.2.b requires students to make use of texts for any one of four interchangeable purposes (build knowledge, develop skills, make informed decisions, share information and ideas). Throughout the lesson, students use the informational text Does the Sun Sleep? to build knowledge about moon patterns. Students answer text-dependent questions such as "What do you notice about the moon's shape over time?" and "What new information does this note provide us?" — articulating what they learned from the text and its diagrams. They then apply that text-derived knowledge in a moon-phase simulation and record observations in their Sky Notebooks. The student-performed purpose (build knowledge from a text) is clearly evidenced, satisfying the clause.

evidence: Invite students to turn and talk with an elbow partner: 'What did you notice about the appearance of the moon as it circled around?'
rationale: The consume clause is partially met: students engage with multiple modalities — an informational book with diagrams (print text + visual text features), a video demonstration ("Play 'Moon Phases Demonstration'"), and a hands-on simulation — and respond to comprehension questions about them (e.g., "What did you notice about the appearance of the moon as it circled around?"). However, the lesson does not ask students to notice or analyze how different genres, text features, or craft techniques are integrated to influence an audience or achieve a purpose; the multimodal consumption is incidental to a science-content objective rather than a deliberate study of multimodal integration. The produce clause is not met: students write observational notes in a Sky Notebook (describing a photograph with an adjective and a preposition), which is a single-mode written response, not a production of a multimodal text that combines genres, text features, and craft techniques to influence a target audience.
